title: Global Funds Are Quietly Returning to Indian Stocks — and the Data Shows the Tide May Finally Be Turning
excerpt: Oil's 42% crash, a rupee rebound, and aggressive RBI reforms have eased the two biggest headwinds that drove $23 billion in foreign selling since 2025
body:
Global fund managers are quietly reassessing their retreat from Indian equities — and for the first time in months, the data suggests the tide may actually be turning.

Exchange data shows that daily selling by foreign institutional investors has slowed markedly in recent weeks. More significantly, analysis by Elara Capital reveals that inflows into U.S.-listed India-focused exchange-traded funds turned positive last week for the first time in over a month. The shift comes as two of the biggest headwinds that had driven foreign capital out of India — surging oil prices and a weakening rupee — have eased in rapid succession.

"Two key headwinds have eased," said Todd McClone, a portfolio manager at William Blair Investment Management, which oversees about $65 billion. "India is among the most oversold markets we track. This macro improvement, alongside a more attractive valuation premium, strengthens the case to act."

What Changed

The catalyst is oil. India imports nearly 90% of its crude requirements, making it one of the world's most vulnerable economies to the Middle East oil shock that began when the Iran conflict escalated in April. Brent crude surged past $126 a barrel at the crisis peak. It has since collapsed 42%, trading around $73 on Tuesday — below pre-war levels — as a fragile U.S.-Iran interim peace deal eased supply fears.

> ""Two key headwinds have eased," said Todd McClone, a portfolio manager at William Blair Investment Management, which oversees about $65 billion."

The rupee has tracked the relief. After plunging to a record low near 97 per dollar in May, the currency recovered to 94.66 by Tuesday's close, posting its first quarterly gain in five quarters. Goldman Sachs has responded by raising its 2026 India growth forecast by 30 basis points and now projects a balance-of-payments surplus of 0.7% of GDP.

The Reserve Bank of India has also moved aggressively: extending a subsidised forex swap facility for banks' overseas borrowings, allowing lenders to extend credit to non-residents against foreign-currency deposits, and scrapping the 12.5% long-term capital gains tax and 20% withholding tax on foreign bond interest income — measures that helped attract a record $3 billion in bond inflows in June alone.

How Deep Was the Exodus?

The scale of foreign selling that preceded this reversal was historic. Average allocations to India among emerging market funds dropped below 10% in April — for the first time since early 2021, down from a peak of 17.5% in August 2024, according to Copley Fund Research. Foreign investors net sold nearly $23 billion of Indian stocks between January 2025 and mid-2026.

India's fall from favour coincided with a global rotation into technology-heavy markets. South Korea and Taiwan emerged as the primary beneficiaries of the AI boom, while stretched Indian valuations gave foreign portfolio managers an easy reason to exit. Domestic investors, however, stepped in to absorb the selling — preventing a more severe market downturn and underscoring the structural depth of India's investor base.

What NRI Investors Should Watch

The Indian benchmark indices reflect the improved backdrop. The Sensex gained 2.3% in June and the Nifty 50 rose 1.4%, with banking stocks leading the charge — the Nifty Bank index surged 6.1% on the month. Pharma gained 4%. The IT index, however, fell 9.6%, weighed down by Accenture's weak demand forecast, AI disruption fears, and expectations that the U.S. Federal Reserve could raise rates later this year as inflation gauges jumped.

For NRI investors evaluating re-entry, the opportunity is real but not without risk. The positives are clear: oil is dramatically lower, the rupee has stabilised, policy reforms are attracting capital, and valuations have come down from the premiums that deterred buyers in 2024. Amundi, Europe's largest asset manager with $2.7 trillion under management, maintains a "structural overweight" on Indian equities, arguing that India's share in global portfolios still doesn't reflect its growth trajectory.

But risks remain. A weak monsoon — June rainfall is running at a 43% deficit — could hurt consumption and rural demand. U.S. inflation data has been stronger than expected, raising the prospect of Fed rate hikes that would strengthen the dollar and pressure emerging market currencies. And the U.S.-Iran détente remains fragile; any escalation could send oil right back up.

"The combination of lower crude, rupee stability and measures to draw foreign inflows has improved sentiment and liquidity," said Ajit Banerjee, chief investment officer at Shriram Life Insurance. "Markets should look better from the second half if no new risks emerge."

The message for NRI investors: the bottom may be in, but selectivity matters. Banks, pharma, and domestic consumption plays look better positioned than export-facing IT and metals. And as always, the monsoon will have the final say on how India's second half unfolds.

*Sources: Reuters (June 30, 2026), Elara Capital, Copley Fund Research, Goldman Sachs, Amundi Investment Institute, Reserve Bank of India*
